lead: Accessible identification is part of how people navigate a building, and it needs a deliberate place in the sign schedule. Tactile characters, braille, visual contrast and placement should be reviewed together with the room’s purpose and the applicable requirements. Vision Graphics can help organize a New York project’s sign list and visual direction for review by the responsible professionals. This page introduces the planning conversation; it does not certify a building or replace an accessibility assessment for the specific property.

sections.html: Identify permanent rooms, entrances, facilities and directional messages using the architect’s or property team’s approved naming. Keep a record of which sign type belongs at each location. Changes to room use or numbering should be resolved before the final text is converted into production artwork.

Have the responsible designer or code professional confirm the applicable criteria and placement details. The proof should identify text, tactile elements, braille, colors and mounting information for review. Field conditions matter: a correctly made panel can still be unsuitable if placed incorrectly.

sections.h2: Build a sign family that can be maintained
sections.html: A coordinated family can include permanent room identification, restroom signs and supporting visual directions. Keep room names, numbers, finishes and sign IDs consistent across the schedule. Distinguish information that is permanent from staff names or other content that may change. Store the approved specification so later replacements can be reviewed against the same design intent.

The number of signs, number of unique messages, panel construction, finish, tactile and braille content, proof revisions and mounting scope affect the quote. Reusing a coordinated layout can simplify design review, but each message still needs approval. Include removal of old signs, wall repairs, restricted work hours and any site verification in the scope discussion.

Share a floor plan, a sign schedule with location IDs, final room names and numbers, and the specifications supplied by the responsible project professional. Include reference photos, branding, existing sign samples if matching is needed, and the installation contact. Agree who approves content, the technical specification and placement. Production should follow the approved schedule rather than assumptions drawn from a photograph.

items.p: Coordinate approved room names and numbers, visual layout, tactile content and braille within the project sign schedule.
Develop the specified visual and tactile layouts for designated facilities, with the final messages and locations approved by the project team.
Align visual directions with room identification while allowing for the different requirements that may apply to each sign type.
Review an existing specification and create a clear schedule for replacement panels or successive areas of work. Matching appearance does not replace technical review.

items.q: Does a braille sign automatically meet every requirement?
items.a_html: No. Content, character treatment, visual qualities and placement must be assessed against the requirements that apply to the project.
The responsible project professional should approve the applicable requirements and final schedule. A product description alone is not a compliance certification.

items.q: Can you match or replace our existing room signs?
items.a_html: Share clear photographs, dimensions, the original specification if available and the list of signs to replace. We can review the visual match and production approach. The responsible professional should confirm the requirements for the replacement signs and their locations.

items.q: What is needed to quote several floors of signs?
items.a_html: A floor plan and a spreadsheet listing each sign ID, message, quantity, location and sign type are useful starting points. Include the approved specification, desired finish and installation responsibilities. Mark unresolved room names or locations so they can be settled before production.
